title: THE MAYORS
canon: An eleven-episode forensic documentary tracing New York City's 75-year fall through the eleven mayors who governed it, 1950 to the present — from Vincent Impellitteri's post-war heights to Zohran Mamdani's Democratic Socialist administration, told alongside one Sicilian immigrant family's parallel story. Shot cinema verite in New York City; the archive is the story, and Episode 11 films the new administration in real time. Who killed New York City? This is the report.
look: Ric Burns-homage documentary realism, forensic not hysterical: each era is rendered in its own period-correct photographic stock — 1950s newsreel black-and-white, early-Kodachrome color, pushed 1970s color negative, gritty 35mm street photography, clean present-day digital cinema. No sets for the present day: New York City IS the set. Light is always motivated by real sources visible or implied in the frame — sky, streetlamps, fire, fluorescents, press flashes — never stylized from nowhere.
note: Six frames spanning the series arc 1952-2026, mirroring the canon's Episode 1 / Episode 11 reverse structure: the 1952 harbor arrival (the canon's own opening visualization), City Hall at the post-war height, Lindsay walking the streets in 1968, the 1977 blackout fires, the 1980 graffiti subway, and the midnight 2026 inauguration in the City Hall ghost station. Decided by the-mayors-canon-FULL.md (Production Style & Visualization, Episode Guide, Episode 11 Concept A) and the ruled 00a-synopsis / 00b-logline (2026-07-08). Only 4 of 35 existing stills are real photographs; refs are limited to those. Cast-continuity warnings: John Lindsay is a real public figure — the archival press photo d48c62da70821606_image-asset.jpeg carries his likeness and wardrobe; the 2026 frame deliberately features no identifiable politician's face (living subject, property is publicSlate=false pending counsel) — the ghost station carries the moment. graffiti-platform-1980 is authored to replace mayors_hero_v2.jpeg, whose AI signage is garbled; its prompt keeps all wall surfaces tagged-over to avoid legible-signage failure. 2026-07-16: APPENDED the press-history set per Marco's ruling — eleven frames, one per mayor from the canon Episode Guide (the-mayors-canon-FULL.md, title/nickname reference table, Impellitteri 1950 through Mamdani 2026), each showing the mayor BEING PRESS (Story Law: a question landing, a denial mid-sentence, a resignation, a victory claim), era-correct press idiom per the existing per-era texture law (Speed Graphic flashbulb B&W newsreel -> Kodachrome -> 16mm news film -> ENG tube/Betacam video -> HD digital). The 2026 sitting mayor's frame is composed with NO identifiable face (likeness-counsel flag, publicSlate=false pending counsel) — silhouette from behind against the flashes only. Diegetic mastheads permitted in-scene but never dominant; no overlay text anywhere.

stills.notes: The canon's own opening image (Production Style & Visualization: October 1952, ship approaching, Statue of Liberty standing guard). No ref — no recurring cast yet, no standing location; the era texture must read newsreel, not modern drone footage.
stills.prompt: The Narrows of New York Harbor, October 1952 — the crowded open deck of an ocean liner steaming toward Ellis Island, immigrant families pressed against the rail in wool overcoats and headscarves, rope-tied cardboard suitcases at their feet. Beyond the bow, the smoke-hazed towers of lower Manhattan; the Statue of Liberty stands off the port side, half veiled in harbor mist. The light is flat overcast Atlantic morning — the even grey sky is the only source, softly modeling the upturned faces, with a pale glare where the sun tries to burn through the coal haze behind the skyline. A Sicilian teenager in a flat cap leans out over the rail, looking up at the city. Black-and-white 35mm newsreel still, heavy silver-halide grain, deep blacks, slight halation on the sky, full-bleed frame edge to edge. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Refs hold the real building — cupola, colonnade, iron fence line — from the genuine 1919 archival print and the modern location photo; the prompt owns the 1953 dressing. Avoids the invented-facade failure the AI batch stills show.
stills.prompt: New York City Hall, City Hall Park, a weekday morning in summer 1953 — the white marble landmark at the height of the city's post-war confidence. Men in seersucker suits and straw boaters cross the plaza, a police officer in a summer tunic stands at the foot of the wide steps, a hot-dog cart with a striped umbrella waits by the cast-iron fence, gulls over the park elms. The light is hard ten-a.m. summer sun from the southeast, raking across the colonnade and clock cupola so the facade reads bright white against a deep blue sky, crisp short shadows on the bluestone plaza; no artificial light anywhere in the frame. Early-Kodachrome large-format color still, saturated primaries, fine grain, gentle lens vignette, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Ref carries John Lindsay's face, build and shirtsleeve wardrobe from a genuine archival press photo — cast continuity for a real public figure; the prompt owns the night-street composition. Avoids the generic-politician failure.
stills.prompt: East Harlem, New York, a hot April night in 1968 — Mayor John Lindsay in shirtsleeves and a loosened tie walks the center of the avenue through an anxious crowd, tall and hatless among residents and a few plainclothes aides. Storefront gates are half down; young men watch from a tenement stoop; glass glitters in the gutter. The light comes from three real sources: greenish mercury-vapor streetlamps overhead, the hot handheld sun-gun of a single TV news crew backpedaling in front of him, and a faint orange glow from a fire some blocks away reflected in the shop windows. Grainy 35mm photojournalism still, Ektachrome pushed two stops, slight motion blur at the frame edges, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Episode 4 territory — 'Drop Dead,' the fiscal-crisis city at bottom. No ref: no cast, and the frame's power is the light law itself — a blacked-out city lit only by its own fires.
stills.prompt: Bushwick, Brooklyn, the night of July 13, 1977 — the citywide blackout. A block of nineteenth-century tenements burns at the right edge of frame while figures carry furniture and televisions past parked Plymouths and Chevrolets; a lone fire company's hose arcs into the smoke. Every streetlamp and every window is dead — the only light in the frame is the fire itself: churning orange underlight on the smoke columns and brick faces, the white-hot core of the blaze reflected in shattered shop glass, and one pair of car headlights cutting low across the foreground crowd. High-speed 1970s color negative pushed to its limit, coarse grain, crushed shadows, halated highlights, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Regenerates the current hero (mayors_hero_v2.jpeg, AI with garbled column signage). No ref — the existing image is itself AI and cannot anchor a real location. Prompt keeps every wall and column tagged-over so no legible signage can garble.
stills.prompt: A deep IND express platform beneath Columbus Circle, New York, winter 1980, near midnight — a downtown train rolls in, every car skinned nose to tail in spray-paint pieces. On the platform a night nurse and a transit cop wait far apart; newspaper pages and token stubs litter the wet concrete; every column, wall and sign surface is tagged over with layers of marker and spray so nothing legible remains. The light is the station's own: dim humming fluorescent tubes overhead with half of them dead, the twin headlights of the arriving train pushing cones through steel-dust haze, and the red glow of an exit lamp at the far end of the platform. Gritty 35mm available-light street photograph, Kodachrome 64, deep murky shadows, visible grain, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Episode 11, Concept A — the midnight January 1, 2026 swearing-in held in the abandoned City Hall loop station. Deliberately no identifiable face and no ref: the living mayor's likeness stays out of generated frames while counsel is pending; the ghost station's architecture carries the moment.
stills.prompt: The abandoned City Hall loop subway station, New York, midnight, January 1, 2026 — the 1904 Guastavino-tiled vaults and brass chandeliers of the city's most ornate ghost station, opened for one night for a mayoral inauguration. A small crowd in winter coats fills the curved platform; an empty lectern stands beneath the central arch; the leaded-glass skylights overhead read black against the sleeping street above. The light is real and layered: warm tungsten chandeliers throwing amber pools along the vault, a cool blue edge from a television crew's LED panel at the platform's end, and the strobing white pops of press cameras freezing faces in the crowd — no other source anywhere. Wide composition holding architecture and crowd together, no single face featured. Clean full-frame digital cinema still, Sony Venice look, natural color, shallow depth, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 1 (The Accidental Mayor). Refs hold the real City Hall portico and steps only. The happening: a corruption question landing mid-scrum in the Kefauver era — Impellitteri caught mid-denial, hand half-raised. Historical public figure of the era, canon uses the historical mayor.
stills.prompt: The steps of New York City Hall under the portico, a cold weekday noon in March 1951 — Mayor Vincent Impellitteri, a slight man in a dark overcoat and fedora, stopped halfway down the marble steps by a wall of newspapermen in belted trench coats, a corruption question just landed: his mouth is open mid-denial, one gloved hand half-raised as if to push the question away. A dozen Speed Graphic press cameras thrust toward him, two flashbulbs firing at the instant of exposure; a radio man shoves a chrome microphone on a long cable up under his chin; a wire-service messenger elbows in at the frame edge. The light is hard and honest: flat grey winter overcast overall, the twin flashbulbs blowing out the mayor's face and collar in harsh white while the crowd behind falls into soot-grey halftones. Black-and-white 4x5 press photograph, newsreel-era silver-halide grain, blown flash highlights, deep blacks, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 2 (The Builder). The happening: Wagner's June 1965 announcement that he will not seek a fourth term — the room reacting, reporters bolting for the phones. Historical public figure, canon uses the historical mayor. No location ref exists for the Blue Room interior; prompt owns the room.
stills.prompt: The Blue Room of New York City Hall, a June morning in 1965 — Mayor Robert F. Wagner Jr., heavy-browed in a dark summer-weight suit, stands at a cluster of chrome microphones having just said he will not run again: his hands are spread flat on the lectern in finality while the room breaks — two reporters already twisting out of their folding chairs toward the door and the phone bank, a photographer vaulting the front row, an aide behind the mayor staring at the floor. Cigarette smoke hangs in a layer at head height. The light is real and layered: tall windows throwing soft daylight across the powder-blue walls and gilt-framed portraits, a pair of hot tungsten newsreel lamps on stands crossing the lectern from both sides, and one flashbulb firing at the instant of exposure. Early-Kodachrome press still, saturated but smoke-dulled color, fine grain, slight tungsten warmth on the mayor against cooler daylight, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 3 (The Liberal Experiment). Ref carries John Lindsay's face and build from the genuine archival press photo — cast continuity for a real public figure; the prompt owns the snow-crisis composition. The happening: the February 1969 Queens snowstorm walk, jeers landing while the cameras roll.
stills.prompt: A residential side street in Fresh Meadows, Queens, February 1969, three days after the great snowstorm — Mayor John Lindsay, tall and hatless in an overcoat, walks a half-plowed street of buried cars while the block turns on him: a woman in curlers and a housecoat jabs a finger at him from her stoop mid-shout, men with snow shovels stand arms-crossed, and the mayor's jaw is set in a grimace as the jeer lands. A 16mm news crew backpedals in front of him — soundman's boom swinging, the camera's battery sun-gun blasting hard white light into his face against the grey afternoon — while two print photographers scramble over a snowbank for the angle. The light is winter-flat overcast off the snow, everything cool and shadowless except the brutal warm-white cone of the sun-gun on the mayor. 16mm color news film frame, Ektachrome news stock pushed a stop, coarse grain, slight gate weave softness at the edges, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 4 (Drop Dead). The happening: October 30, 1975 — Beame holding up that morning's Daily News front page in fury at a City Hall pressroom lectern. Diegetic masthead permitted per ruling but held at an angle, small in frame, partially caught by flash — it must not dominate; the mayor's anger is the subject.
stills.prompt: The cramped press room of New York City Hall, Room 9, the morning of October 30, 1975 — Mayor Abraham Beame, a small silver-haired man dwarfed by the lectern, holds up a folded tabloid newspaper at arm's length like evidence at a trial, his other fist on the lectern, face flushed mid-sentence in genuine anger; the paper is angled away from camera, its headline caught only as a partial glare of black type in the flash. Before him a crush of reporters in wide-lapel suits shout over each other, pencils up, cassette recorders thrust forward; a TV cameraman's 16mm rig hangs over the scrum from a chair. The light is grim municipal fluorescent — greenish tubes overhead flattening everyone — ruptured by two strobes firing at once, hard white on the mayor and the raised paper. 1970s color-negative press photograph pushed for the dim room, coarse grain, fluorescent green-grey cast against blown flash whites, crushed shadows, full-bleed frame. No text overlay, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 5 (The Comeback Kid). The happening: the April 1980 transit strike — Koch on the Brooklyn Bridge walkway playing the press like an instrument, mid-victory-taunt at the strikers as commuters cheer. ENG-era texture begins here per the era law.
stills.prompt: The wooden pedestrian walkway of the Brooklyn Bridge, a bright cold April morning in 1980, day three of the transit strike — Mayor Ed Koch, balding and beaming in a raincoat, arms flung wide mid-taunt, playing to a river of commuters walking to work as they cheer him; one businesswoman in sneakers pumps her fist back at him. A shoulder-mounted ENG video crew walks backward two feet in front of his face, correspondent's wired microphone under his chin, while a second crew shoots across from the cable rail and a print photographer crouches for the low hero angle against the bridge towers. The light is hard morning sun off the East River raking down the walkway boards, deep cable shadows striping the crowd, plus the small hot fill of the ENG rig's battery light on the mayor's face. Early ENG tube-camera video frame grab, slight comet-tail smear on the sun glints, muted saturated color, scanline softness, 4:3-era framing feel within a full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 6 (The Safe Streets Debate). The happening: Crown Heights, August 1991 — Dinkins mobbed mid-plea on the street, the crowd's fury and a thrown bottle in the air while the cameras press in. Historical public figure, canon uses the historical mayor.
stills.prompt: President Street, Crown Heights, Brooklyn, a humid August night in 1991 — Mayor David Dinkins, dignified in shirtsleeves, a bullhorn half-raised, is pressed on all sides in the middle of the street mid-plea for calm as the crowd jeers; a plastic bottle hangs in the air above the scrum, thrown from somewhere behind the police line, and a plainclothes detective is already reaching to pull the mayor back by the shoulder. Betacam news crews shove in from both sides, their camera-top lights carving hot white wedges through the dark; a boom mic dips into frame; NYPD portable barricades and a blue-and-white cruiser strobe at the frame edge. The light is all real and ugly: sodium-vapor orange streetlamps overhead, the cruiser's red-and-blue flicker on faces, and the ENG camera lights blasting the mayor flat white against the dark crowd. Betacam ENG video frame grab, smeared highlights, muddy shadows, video-noise grain in the blacks, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 7 (Broken Windows / September Eleven). The happening: the morning of September 11, 2001 — Giuliani walking north through the dust with a gaggle of reporters, answering on the move. Composed sober and forensic per the canon's Ric Burns register; no bodies, no towers falling in frame — the dust and the walking press conference carry it.
stills.prompt: Church Street, lower Manhattan, mid-morning, September 11, 2001 — Mayor Rudy Giuliani strides north through a fog of grey-white dust, suit shoulders powdered, a respirator mask hanging unused at his neck, answering a question over his shoulder mid-stride; around him a moving knot of reporters and aides keeps pace, one correspondent holding a microphone across another's shoulder, a photographer walking backward shooting blind, a police captain gesturing the group up the street. Paper and ash drift like snow; abandoned shoes and a crushed coffee cart stand at the curb. The light is apocalyptic but real: the sun reduced to a pale disc through the dust canopy, everything a single toneless grey-white, with the one hot exception of a Betacam's camera light punching through the haze onto the mayor's dust-caked face. Betacam SP news video frame grab, blown soft highlights in the dust, desaturated near-monochrome color, handheld motion blur at the frame edges, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 8 (The Technocrat). The happening: October 2008, the Blue Room — the term-limits extension announcement, the question 'you're overturning two referendums?' landing and Bloomberg's dismissive mid-sentence wave. Historical public figure, canon uses the historical mayor.
stills.prompt: The Blue Room of New York City Hall, October 2008 — Mayor Michael Bloomberg, compact in a charcoal suit at a modern lectern flanked by flags, gives a curt dismissive flick of the hand mid-sentence as a shouted question about overturning the voters' term limits lands; his mouth is tight, half-turned from the room. Before him the front row bristles: a wire reporter half-standing with her recorder thrust out, laptops open on knees, a bank of tripod-mounted broadcast cameras at the rear with their red tally lights on, still photographers kneeling in the aisle firing. The light is institutional and clean: the room's warm tungsten downlight on the powder-blue walls and portraits, crossed by the flat white of TV lights on stands and the intermittent hard pops of speedlights off the ceiling. Early HD broadcast still, clinical clean color, slight video sharpness, deep depth of field, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 9 (Tale of Two Cities). The happening: March 16, 2020 — the press ambush outside the Prospect Park YMCA, the 'why are you at the gym' question landing as the city shuts down. Historical public figure, canon uses the historical mayor.
stills.prompt: The sidewalk outside the Prospect Park YMCA on Ninth Street, Park Slope, Brooklyn, the grey morning of March 16, 2020 — Mayor Bill de Blasio, very tall in a half-zipped fleece with a gym bag on his shoulder, caught between the YMCA door and his black SUV by a half-circle of reporters in the first surgical masks of the pandemic; the question about why he is at the gym while the city shuts down has just landed and his palms are up mid-justification, shoulders hunched. A phone-camera on a gimbal is a foot from his face; a masked photographer shoots one-handed; his security detail holds the SUV door open, urging him in; the street behind is unnervingly empty. The light is flat overcast pandemic-spring daylight, shadowless and cold, with a single small LED panel from a video crew adding an off-white edge on the mayor's face. Modern HD mirrorless press photograph, clean digital color held slightly desaturated, deep focus, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 10 (The Reckoning / The Indicted Mayor). The happening: September 26, 2024 — the defiant Gracie Mansion statement after the federal indictment, a heckler's 'resign' landing mid-sentence. Historical public figure, canon uses the historical mayor.
stills.prompt: The front lawn of Gracie Mansion, East End Avenue, Manhattan, the grey morning of September 26, 2024 — Mayor Eric Adams at a small outdoor lectern before the mansion's yellow clapboard facade, mid-defiant-sentence the day of his federal indictment, chin raised, finger pressed to the lectern top; at the edge of the press pen a heckler's shout of resignation is landing — heads in the press corps turning toward the shout while the mayor keeps talking through it. The pen is jammed: boom mics, a thicket of phone rigs and shotgun mics taped to a lectern-mounted mic tree, network cameras on tripods in a rear rank, stills shooters at the rope. The light is soft overcast bounced off the pale house, with two broadcast LED panels crossing the mayor warm-white and a speedlight popping at the instant of exposure. HD digital-cinema press still, clean natural color, shallow-medium depth isolating the lectern against the softened facade, full-bleed frame. No text, no watermark.

stills.notes: Press-history set, Episode 11 (The Socialist Experiment). LIKENESS-COUNSEL FLAG: the sitting 2026 mayor must NOT be identifiable in any generated frame (property is publicSlate=false pending counsel; same law as midnight-oath-2026). Composed entirely from behind the lectern — the mayor is a dark silhouette against the wall of flashes; no facial features, no profile. The happening: the first hostile scrum of the new administration, the room's hands all up at once.
stills.prompt: The Blue Room of New York City Hall, a winter afternoon in 2026 — shot from directly behind the lectern, over the dark-coated shoulders and back of the new mayor, who is a clean anonymous silhouette against the room: no face, no profile, only hands gripping the lectern edges and a sheaf of briefing papers curling under one thumb. Beyond the silhouette the room erupts — every reporter's hand up at once, mouths open mid-shout, a forest of phones and shotgun mics tilting forward, the rear rank of broadcast cameras with red tally lights burning. The light logic makes the anonymity: the massed TV panels and a ripple of camera flashes fire straight into the lens from across the room, silhouetting the mayor in hard rim light while the press corps is fully lit; a haze of winter radiator heat catches the beams. Clean full-frame digital cinema still, Sony Venice look, high-contrast backlight exposure holding the silhouette pure black, full-bleed frame. No identifiable person at the lectern. No text, no watermark.
